transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. Well, I guess what brings me in is this... constant restless feeling I have. It's like I'm wound too tight, and I just can't fully settle down. Even when I'm supposed to be doing something calm, like sitting through a planning meeting for work, or... or even when I'm trying to relax by painting or doing yoga. I just can't seem to settle.

When you feel this restless and wound-up feeling, do you also find yourself worrying a lot about things, or does your mood feel different in other ways—like feeling down, or unusually energetic or irritable?

No, I wouldn't say I worry a lot. It's not an anxious feeling, really. And I don't feel down or depressed. I'm just... fidgety. I don't feel unusually energetic or irritable either, just like I can't stay still. It's more physical than emotional, I guess.
When did you first start noticing this restless, fidgety feeling? Has it been present since you were a child, or did it start more recently in your adult years?

It's definitely been there since I was a kid. I remember back in elementary school, my parents would actually get notes sent home from my teachers about it. The notes usually said that I kept popping out of my seat during class, or that I was talking over my classmates. I also had a habit of... well, I'd just rush to answer before the teacher had even finished asking the question. So, yeah, it's been this way for a long time, definitely not something that just started in my adult years.
Besides the fidgeting and restlessness, do you also have trouble focusing or concentrating on tasks—like difficulty keeping your attention on work, reading, or conversations?

No, not really. I mean, I don't have any major problems paying attention. If I'm reading a report for work or talking with someone, I can focus just fine. It's really just the physical part—the needing to move or do something with my hands—that bothers me. But my concentration itself seems okay.
Do you find it difficult to organize your tasks or complete projects, or do you tend to act impulsively without thinking things through first?

No, I don't really have trouble organizing my tasks. In my job as a buyer, I have to keep track of a lot of moving parts, so I'm actually pretty good at staying on top of things and finishing my projects. 

And as for acting impulsively... no, I wouldn't say I do that either. I mean, I know I mentioned blurting out answers in school when I was younger, but as far as actually doing things without thinking them through first today, I haven't really noticed that being an issue. Like I said, it's mostly just that restless physical feeling for me.

When you're working on a task that requires sustained attention, like reading through a detailed report or following a complex conversation, do you ever find yourself getting distracted by things around you, or do your thoughts tend to wander even though you're trying to concentrate?

No, I don't really have that problem. Like I was saying before, my focus is generally fine. If I'm reading through a detailed report for work or having a conversation, I can stay with it. I don't really get distracted by things around me or find my mind wandering off. I can concentrate when I need to.

When you were in school as a child, besides the fidgeting and popping out of your seat, did your teachers also mention problems with you paying attention, staying on task, or forgetting instructions—or was it really just about the physical restlessness and talking?

No, from what I remember, it was really just the physical stuff. My teachers didn't have any complaints about me paying attention or forgetting instructions. I did fine with the actual assignments and getting my work done. It was always just... you know, them telling me to sit still or stop talking. So yeah, staying on task wasn't really the issue back then either.

latest_inference.note: Lifelong history of motor restlessness and fidgeting since childhood, with teacher reports of difficulty sitting still and impulsivity (blurting out answers). No significant inattention, no organizational problems, no impulsivity in decision-making, and no hyperactivity/energy elevation. This presentation is consistent with Predominantly Hyperactive-Impulsive Type ADHD. Other conditions ruled out: no anxiety disorder features, no mood disorder, no thought disorder.
